title: What can you say about digestive enzymes in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 3 wordings for digestive enzymes; the strongest is "Helps digest lactose, the sugar in milk and dairy foods" (strong, 3,000-54,000 FCC ALU lactase activity a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Prevents or treats lactose intolerance".

supported_wordings.wording: Helps digest lactose, the sugar in milk and dairy foods.
supported_wordings.why: Authorized in the EU after EFSA review and listed by Health Canada at overlapping doses.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: 3,000-54,000 FCC ALU lactase activity a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Health Canada: 3,000-54,000 FCC ALU a day, at most 18,000 per dose, adults 18 and older. EU: at least 4,500 FCC units with each lactose-containing meal, for people who have difficulty digesting lactose.

sources.name: Commission Regulation (EU) No 432/2012, list of permitted health claims

supported_wordings.wording: Helps reduce gas after meals rich in beans, vegetables or whole grains.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it at 260-3,000 FCC GalU a day; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: 260-3,000 FCC GalU alpha-galactosidase activity a day

supported_wordings.wording: Helps reduce bloating after large, high-fat meals.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada lists it for pancreatic enzymes; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.dose_details: Health Canada, pancreatic enzymes, adults 18 and older: lipase 5,000-40,000 USP units a day (at most 20,000 per dose), amylase 17,000-149,000 (at most 37,000 per dose) and protease 16,000-125,000 (at most 38,000 per dose).

wordings_to_avoid.why: Names a diagnosable condition. Both the EU and Health Canada support wording about digesting lactose, which is the safer framing.
Names a disease or a symptom of one.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Replaces prescription pancreatic enzymes, or helps with pancreatic insufficiency
wordings_to_avoid.why: Presents the product as a substitute for a prescription drug and names a disease.
Promises to relieve a medical problem. Health Canada lists bromelain for minor pain, swelling and inflammation, but that is treatment wording.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

sources.name: Commission Regulation (EU) No 432/2012, list of permitted health claims

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
